{{Short description|In algebra}}
In [[algebra]], '''Zariski's lemma''', proved by {{harvs|txt|first=Oscar|last= Zariski|authorlink=Oscar Zariski|year=1947}}, states that, if a [[field (mathematics)|field]] ''K'' is [[finitely generated algebra|finitely generated]] as an [[associative algebra]] over another field ''k'', then ''K'' is a [[finite field extension]] of ''k''; that is, ''K'' is finitely generated as a [[Module (mathematics)|module]] (in other words, ''K'' is a finite dimensional [[vector space]]) over ''k''.

An important application of the lemma is a proof of the weak form of [[Hilbert's Nullstellensatz]]:{{sfn|Milne|2017|loc=Theorem 2.12}} if ''I'' is a proper [[ideal (ring theory)|ideal]] of <math>k[t_1, ..., t_n]</math> (''k'' an [[algebraically closed field]]), then ''I'' has a zero; i.e., there is a point ''x'' in <math>k^n</math> such that <math>f(x) = 0</math> for all ''f'' in ''I''. (Proof: replacing ''I'' by a [[maximal ideal]] <math>\mathfrak{m}</math>, we can assume <math>I = \mathfrak{m}</math> is maximal. Let <math>A = k[t_1, ..., t_n]</math> and <math>\phi: A \to A / \mathfrak{m}</math> be the natural surjection. By the lemma <math>A / \mathfrak{m}</math> is a finite extension. Since ''k'' is algebraically closed that extension must be ''k''. Then for any <math>f \in \mathfrak{m}</math>,
:<math>f(\phi(t_1), \cdots, \phi(t_n)) = \phi(f(t_1, \cdots, t_n)) = 0</math>;
that is to say, <math>x = (\phi(t_1), \cdots, \phi(t_n))</math> is a zero of <math>\mathfrak{m}</math>.)

The lemma may also be understood from the following perspective. In general, a ring ''R'' is a [[Jacobson ring]] if and only if every finitely generated ''R''-algebra that is a field is finite over ''R''.{{sfn|Atiyah|MacDonald|1969|loc=Ch 5. Exercise 25}} Thus, the lemma follows from the fact that a field is a Jacobson ring.

== Proofs ==
Two direct proofs are given in Atiyah–MacDonald;{{sfn|Atiyah|MacDonald|1969|loc=Ch 5. Exercise 18}}{{sfn|Atiyah|MacDonald|1969|loc=Proposition 7.9}} the one is due to Zariski and the other uses the [[Artin–Tate lemma]]. For Zariski's original proof, see the original paper.{{sfn|Zariski|1947|pp=362–368}} Another direct proof in the language of [[Jacobson ring]]s is given below. The lemma is also a consequence of the [[Noether normalization lemma]]. Indeed, by the normalization lemma, ''K'' is a [[finitely generated module|finite module]] over the polynomial ring <math>k[x_1, \ldots , x_d]</math> where <math>x_1, \ldots , x_d</math> are elements of ''K'' that are algebraically independent over ''k''. But since ''K'' has [[Krull dimension]] zero and since an [[integral ring extension]] (e.g., a [[finite ring]] extension) preserves Krull dimensions, the [[polynomial ring]] must have dimension zero; i.e., <math>d=0</math>.

The following characterization of a Jacobson ring contains Zariski's lemma as a special case. Recall that a ring is a Jacobson ring if every [[prime ideal]] is an intersection of maximal ideals. (When ''A'' is a field, ''A'' is a Jacobson ring and the theorem below is precisely Zariski's lemma.)

{{math theorem|math_statement={{sfn|Atiyah|MacDonald|1969|loc=Ch 5. Exercise 25}} Let ''A'' be a ring. Then the following are equivalent.
# ''A'' is a Jacobson ring.
# Every finitely generated ''A''-algebra ''B'' that is a field is finite over ''A''.
}}

Proof: 2. <math>\Rightarrow</math> 1.: Let <math>\mathfrak{p}</math> be a prime ideal of ''A'' and set <math>B = A/\mathfrak{p}</math>. We need to show the [[Jacobson radical]] of ''B'' is zero. For that end, let ''f'' be a nonzero element of ''B''. Let <math>\mathfrak{m}</math> be a maximal ideal of the localization <math>B[f^{-1}]</math>. Then <math>B[f^{-1}]/\mathfrak{m}</math> is a field that is a finitely generated ''A''-algebra and so is finite over ''A'' by assumption; thus it is finite over <math>B = A/\mathfrak{p}</math> and so is finite over the [[subring]] <math>B/\mathfrak{q}</math> where <math>\mathfrak{q} = \mathfrak{m} \cap B</math>. By integrality, <math>\mathfrak{q}</math> is a maximal ideal not containing ''f''.

1. <math>\Rightarrow</math> 2.: Since a factor ring of a Jacobson ring is Jacobson, we can assume ''B'' contains ''A'' as a subring. Then the assertion is a consequence of the next algebraic fact:

:(*) Let <math>B \supseteq A</math> be integral domains such that ''B'' is finitely generated as ''A''-algebra. Then there exists a nonzero ''a'' in ''A'' such that every [[ring homomorphism]] <math>\phi: A \to K</math>, ''K'' an algebraically closed field, with <math>\phi(a) \ne 0</math> extends to <math>\widetilde{\phi}: B \to K</math>.

Indeed, choose a maximal ideal <math>\mathfrak{m}</math> of ''A'' not containing ''a''. Writing ''K'' for some algebraic closure of <math>A/\mathfrak{m}</math>, the canonical map <math>\phi: A \to A/\mathfrak{m} \hookrightarrow K</math> extends to <math>\widetilde{\phi}: B \to K</math>. Since ''B'' is a field, <math>\widetilde{\phi}</math> is injective and so ''B'' is algebraic (thus finite algebraic) over <math>A/\mathfrak{m}</math>.  We now prove (*). If ''B'' contains an element that is transcendental over ''A'', then it contains a polynomial ring over ''A'' to which ''φ'' extends (without a requirement on ''a'') and so we can assume ''B'' is algebraic over ''A'' (by [[Zorn's lemma]], say). Let <math>x_1, \dots, x_r</math> be the generators of ''B'' as ''A''-algebra. Then each <math>x_i</math> satisfies the relation
:<math>a_{i0}x_i^n + a_{i1}x_i^{n-1} + \dots + a_{in} = 0, \, \, a_{ij} \in A</math>
where ''n'' depends on ''i'' and <math>a_{i0} \ne 0</math>. Set <math>a = a_{10}a_{20} \dots a_{r0}</math>. Then <math>B[a^{-1}]</math> is integral over <math>A[a^{-1}]</math>. Now given <math>\phi: A \to K</math>, we first extend it to <math>\widetilde{\phi}: A[a^{-1}] \to K</math> by setting <math>\widetilde{\phi}(a^{-1}) = \phi(a)^{-1}</math>. Next, let <math>\mathfrak{m} = \operatorname{ker}\widetilde{\phi}</math>. By integrality, <math>\mathfrak{m} = \mathfrak{n} \cap A[a^{-1}]</math> for some maximal ideal <math>\mathfrak{n}</math> of <math>B[a^{-1}]</math>. Then <math>\widetilde{\phi}: A[a^{-1}] \to A[a^{-1}]/\mathfrak{m} \to K</math> extends to <math>B[a^{-1}] \to B[a^{-1}]/\mathfrak{n} \to K</math>. Restrict the last map to ''B'' to finish the proof. <math>\square</math>
